meaning: A short story, often with animals, that teaches a lesson
trick: FABLE - FABLES like Aesop's teach a lesson at the end.
examples: They were like characters in a fable.
The fable of the hare and the tortoise teaches patience.

usage.pattern: a fable about something / the moral of a fable

meaning: A false outward appearance hiding the truth; also the front of a building (also spelled 'façade')
hindi: दिखावा, बाहरी रूप; इमारत का अगला भाग
trick: FACADE - the FACE a building (or person) shows.
examples: They keep their mental facade standing at all costs.
Behind his cheerful facade, he was very sad.

usage.pattern: a facade of something / behind a facade

meaning: The different sides or parts of something
trick: FACETS - like the many FACES of a cut diamond.
examples: It makes you better in all facets of your life.
We discussed all facets of the plan.

meaning: A small group within a larger one, often in conflict with others
trick: FACTION - a FRACTION of the group that fights the rest.
examples: There was heavy fighting between Sayyaf's forces and the Wahdat faction.
A faction of the party refused to vote.

meaning: Relating to fighting or disagreement between groups
trick: FACTIONAL - between FACTIONS.
examples: The Taliban were ending factional war wherever they settled.
Factional fights weakened the club.

meaning: Small groups within a larger one that disagree with each other
trick: FACTIONS - FRACTIONS of a group that pull apart.
examples: The animals formed themselves into two factions.
The party split into two factions.

meaning: A servant or employee who does many different jobs
trick: FACTOTUM - Latin 'do everything': FACT (do) + TOTUM (all).
examples: The undertaker's factotum showed us to our places.
He is the office factotum who fixes everything.

meaning: A natural power of the mind or body; also teachers of a college
trick: FACULTY - your mental FACULTIES are your abilities.
examples: Benjamin could read as well as any pig, but never used his faculty.
She has a great faculty for remembering names.

usage.pattern: a faculty for something / faculty of something

meaning: Offensive slur for gay men; also (old) bundles of sticks for burning
trick: FAGGOTS - old word for bundles of sticks; today a hateful slur, so avoid it.
examples: The bully shouted that they would grow up to be faggots, a hurtful slur.
Old stories say farmers burned faggots of wood in winter.

meaning: Weak or hard to see, hear or notice; also to pass out
trick: FAINT - so FAINT it almost faints away.
examples: There was a faint smile on her lips now.
I heard a faint sound from the next room.

meaning: Fast birds of prey that can be trained to hunt
trick: FALCONS - fast as a FALCON jet.
examples: Shoppers bought oranges, books, shawls, even falcons.
The king kept falcons for hunting.

meaning: The bad results of an event; also radioactive dust after a nuclear blast
trick: FALLOUT - what FALLS OUT after the explosion.
examples: It's your responsibility to manage the emotional fallout of the experience.
The political fallout from the scandal was huge.

meaning: To become weak or unsure; to lose strength or confidence
trick: FALTER - almost FALL but recover.
examples: Your resolution must never falter.
Her voice began to falter as she spoke.

meaning: A moment of weakness or unsteadiness; also unsteady
trick: FALTERING - nearly FALLING, step by step.
examples: He was waiting for a subtle faltering in her breathing.
He spoke in faltering English.

usage.pattern: a faltering + noun / faltering in something

meaning: Known by many people; famous
trick: FAMED = FAMous.
examples: He would show her the famed tree with a poet buried beneath it.
The city is famed for its sweets.

usage.pattern: famed for something / the famed + noun

meaning: A serious lack of food in an area, causing many to starve
trick: FAMINE - FAMished (very hungry) people.
examples: People said the animals were dying of famine and disease.
The famine killed millions of people.

meaning: Thinks of oneself as something, often wrongly; also likes or wants
hindi: समझता है (खुद को); पसंद करता है
trick: FANCIES himself a hero = in his FANCY (imagination).
examples: The husband fancies himself some kind of educated intellectual.
He fancies himself a great cook.

meaning: To want or like something (British informal); also to think or suppose
trick: FANCY a tea? = do you want one?
examples: If you fancy something, I will get it for you.
Do you fancy going to the cinema tonight?

meaning: Moved air towards something with a fan or hand to cool it
trick: FANNED - used a FAN.
examples: He sat beside her cot and fanned her face.
She fanned herself with a newspaper.

meaning: Moving the air with a fan or the hand
trick: FANNING - like a hand FAN going back and forth.
examples: She made a fanning motion with her hand.
He was fanning the coals to light the fire.

meaning: Strange and imaginary; not realistic
trick: FANTASTICAL - from FANTASY land.
examples: It made Laila's promises sound fantastical and foolish.
The book is full of fantastical creatures.

meaning: Acts or words of saying goodbye
trick: FAREWELLS - 'FARE WELL' = travel well.
examples: All around them, farewells were yelled.
We said our farewells at the airport.

meaning: Getting on or doing (well or badly) in a situation
trick: FARE = how you get on; 'How are you faring?' = how are you doing?
examples: My top half wasn't faring much better.
How is your new business faring?

meaning: A harsh, far-right system of rule by a dictator who crushes opposition; also any very controlling, bullying behaviour
trick: FASCISM - Mussolini's Fascists; 'fasces' = bundle of rods = force.
examples: His friends called psychiatry a form of fascism.
Many people died fighting fascism in the Second World War.

usage.pattern: fight against fascism / a form of fascism

meaning: A way or manner of doing something; also the popular style of clothes at a time
trick: 'After their fashion' = in their own style/way.
examples: I thought they were greeting me, after their fashion.
He finished the work in a quick fashion.

usage.pattern: in a … fashion / after someone's fashion

meaning: A death caused by an accident, war or disaster
trick: FATAL + ITY = a fatal event = a death.
examples: Within thirty days of a fatality, the staff reach out to the family.
The crash caused one fatality and two injuries.

meaning: Loose clothes worn by soldiers for work or battle; also (fatigue) great tiredness
trick: Soldiers in FATIGUES get fatigued (tired) doing hard work.
examples: They sat and smoked atop tanks, dressed in their fatigues.
The soldier changed out of his fatigues after training.

meaning: Taps that control the flow of water (American English)
trick: FAUCET sounds like 'four-set' - a set of taps over the sink.
examples: The sink had twin faucets for hot and cold water.
Please turn off the faucets after washing your hands.

meaning: To make someone worried, nervous or confused
trick: FAZE ≠ phase. Nothing FAZEs a calm person - not even a new phase.
examples: My early burst on day three didn't faze him.
Loud noises don't faze my dog at all.

meaning: To eat a lot of something with great enjoyment; also a large special meal
hindi: दावत उड़ाना, जी भरकर खाना; दावत
trick: FEAST = eat like it's a festival.
examples: The hungry dogs found food and began to feast.
We will feast on biryani at the wedding.

meaning: An achievement that needs great skill, strength or courage
trick: FEAT sounds like 'feet' - running a marathon on your feet is a feat.
examples: They think good things happen because of some amazing feat they accomplished.
Climbing Everest is a great feat.

usage.pattern: a feat of something / no mean feat

meaning: Solid waste passed out of the body (American spelling of faeces)
trick: FECES - the 'fecal' matter that goes down the toilet.
examples: There were ditches to dig and feces to shovel from outhouses.
The vet checked the dog's feces for worms.

meaning: Very weak, without strength or force; also not convincing
trick: FEEBLE ~ 'feel-able'? No - too weak to feel anything.
examples: My lawyer struck me as feeble to the point of being ridiculous.
The old man gave a feeble smile.

meaning: Weaker, with less strength or force
trick: FEEBLE + R = more feeble.
examples: The sound of the waves was even lazier, feebler, than at noon.
His voice grew feebler as the night went on.

meaning: To pretend to feel or have something
trick: FEIGN sounds like 'fake' + 'n' - fake it.
examples: She hoped he would deny everything and feign surprise.
He tried to feign illness to skip school.

usage.pattern: feign something / feign to do something

meaning: Having qualities thought typical of women
trick: FEMININE - from 'femina' = woman (female).
examples: He claimed she had seduced him with her feminine charms.
She likes soft, feminine colours like pink.

meaning: A barrier of wood or wire around an area of land
trick: FENCE defends (de-FENCE) your land.
examples: He built a chicken coop with a fence around it.
The cow jumped over the fence.

meaning: To defend yourself from someone or something unwanted
trick: FEND = short for deFEND - defend it off.
examples: Hasina gave advice on how to fend off unattractive suitors.
She used her umbrella to fend off the dog.

meaning: Very fierce, angry or violent
trick: FEROCIOUS - FERAL + ATROCIOUS = wild and terrible.
examples: Mammy was ferocious, pacing and ranting.
The ferocious dog barked at the postman.

meaning: In a very fierce or violent way
trick: FEROCIOUS + LY = in a ferocious way.
examples: The dogs suddenly appeared, baying ferociously.
The two teams fought ferociously for the cup.

meaning: (of soil) able to grow many good crops; also able to have babies
trick: FERTILE land needs FERTILizer.
examples: The soil of England is fertile and its climate is good.
Farmers love this fertile valley.

meaning: Makes soil richer so plants grow well (British spelling of fertilizes)
hindi: खाद देता है, उपजाऊ बनाता है
trick: FERTILISES = adds FERTILISER.
examples: Our labour tills the soil, our dung fertilises it.
My father fertilises the garden every spring.

meaning: Relating to an unborn baby; the curled-up position = lying with knees pulled to the chest
trick: FETAL - from 'fetus', the curled-up baby in the womb.
examples: I would always wake in the fetal position on the floor.
The scan showed healthy fetal growth.

usage.pattern: in the fetal position / fetal + noun

meaning: Went to get something and brought it back
trick: FETCH - 'Go fetch!' you tell a dog.
examples: He went around the back of the shed and fetched a ladder.
She fetched a glass of water for her grandmother.

meaning: Like a feudal lord: ruling an area with personal power, as in old times
trick: FEUD-al = old lords who owned the land and the people on it.
examples: Herat's feudal-style warlord has helped rebuild the city.
The village was run in a feudal-style way by one rich family.

meaning: A fast, irregular quivering of the heart muscle
trick: FIBRILLATION - the heart's fibres flutter (fib-rill) instead of beating.
examples: My heart went into atrial fibrillation, also known as a-fib.
The doctor treated his fibrillation with medicine.

meaning: To keep making small restless movements
trick: FIDGET - fidget spinners keep restless fingers busy.
examples: Raymond was beginning to fidget.
Children fidget when they have to sit still too long.

meaning: Kept making small restless movements
trick: FIDGET + ED - he fidgeted on his chair.
examples: He fidgeted to and fro, swishing his long black tail.
She fidgeted with her pen during the exam.

meaning: Very strong, intense or violent
trick: FIERCE like a fire - hot and strong.
examples: A fierce battle was under way there.
There is fierce competition for the job.

meaning: Looking angry, strong or frightening
trick: FIERCE + LOOKING = looks like it might bite.
examples: Napoleon was a large, rather fierce-looking boar.
A fierce-looking guard stood at the gate.

meaning: Like fire, burning; also full of strong emotion, passionate
trick: FIERY = fire-y.
examples: Their anger rained down all at once, like a fiery hailstorm.
He gave a fiery speech to the crowd.

meaning: Something that seems real but is only imagined
trick: FIGMENT ~ 'fig-ment' - a fake fruit of your mind.
examples: Your supposed superiority is a figment of your own ego.
The ghost was just a figment of her imagination.

meaning: Soft, sweet, pear-shaped fruits full of small seeds, often eaten dried
trick: FIGS - 'anjeer'; dried figs in a dry-fruit box.
examples: Mariam packed Zalmai a small lunch of bread and dried figs.
My mother soaks figs in water overnight.

meaning: Walked out one after another in a line
trick: FILE = a line (single file) - they filed out in a line.
examples: The priest, the boys, and I filed out.
The students filed out of the classroom quietly.

meaning: Relating to the duty or love of a son or daughter towards parents
trick: FILIAL - from Latin 'filius' = son.
examples: They had an almost filial respect for Clover.
Caring for old parents is a filial duty in India.

meaning: Cut open or sliced deeply, like meat; also (of fish) with the bones removed
trick: FILLET a fish = slice it open with a knife.
examples: His palms were filleted open by the sharp rocks.
The cook served filleted fish with rice.

meaning: Disgusting dirt; also rude or offensive language
trick: FILTH = full of dirt - FILTHy.
examples: They washed away the bodily filth of strangers down the drain.
The street was covered in filth after the flood.

usage.pattern: covered in filth / live in filth

meaning: Getting something in a clever, dishonest way (informal)
trick: FINAGLING - a 'fine angle' to cheat someone.
examples: He made money by finagling a loan from someone.
She is finagling free tickets from her friend.

meaning: Small songbirds with short thick beaks for eating seeds
trick: FINCHES - like little chicks that sing.
examples: The porcelain had hand-painted finches and chrysanthemums.
Two finches were eating seeds at the feeder.

meaning: Very thin or delicate; also good, or money paid as a punishment
trick: FINE thread = so thin it's fine and delicate.
examples: The sleeves were embroidered with fine red and yellow silk thread.
She has fine, soft hair.

meaning: The ends of the fingers
trick: FINGER + TIPS = the tips of your fingers.
examples: She washed laundry in the cold until her fingertips burned.
He touched the screen with his fingertips.

usage.pattern: at your fingertips / with your fingertips

meaning: Swimming by moving fins or flippers, or arms and feet like fins
trick: FIN-NING = using your limbs like fish fins.
examples: Soon finning with my arms or feet became easy for me.
The diver was finning slowly along the reef.

meaning: Thin flat parts on a fish's body that help it swim
trick: FINS - Nemo has one small fin.
examples: Fish don't wonder if they'd be liked more with longer fins.
The shark's fins showed above the water.

meaning: Guns that can be carried, like pistols and rifles
trick: FIRE + ARMS = weapons that fire.
examples: The animals must get firearms and train in their use.
Firearms are not allowed on the plane.

meaning: Searched for and pulled something out of a pocket or bag
trick: FISHED - like fishing: reach in and pull something out.
examples: He fished a sky blue burqa from the bag.
She fished her keys out of her purse.

meaning: Amounts that can be held in a closed hand
trick: FIST + FULS = as much as a fist holds.
examples: Her hands clenched the sheets in fistfuls.
The child grabbed fistfuls of sweets.

meaning: Not steady; stopping and starting, often used about sleep
trick: FITFUL - comes in FITS and starts.
examples: She had fitful dreams about the jinn.
After the news, he had a fitful night's sleep.

meaning: (of a gate) made with five horizontal bars
trick: FIVE-BARRED gate = five bars across, a classic farm gate.
examples: The men had entered the five-barred gate.
He climbed over the five-barred gate into the field.

meaning: Arranged or organised something; also repaired
hindi: तय कर लिया, इंतज़ाम किया; ठीक किया
trick: FIXED UP = fixed a plan, all set.
examples: I have fixed up with my employer for two days' leave.
She fixed up a meeting with the manager.

meaning: Extremely surprised or shocked
trick: FLABBERGASTED - so shocked you GASP and your jaw goes flabby.
examples: For a bit Céleste seemed flabbergasted.
I was flabbergasted by the huge bill.

meaning: Soft and hanging loosely, not firm
trick: FLACCID ~ 'flab-cid' - flabby and floppy.
examples: The flag fell flaccid when the wind stopped.
The balloon was flaccid by morning.

meaning: A tall pole on which a flag is flown
trick: FLAG + STAFF (stick) = flag stick.
examples: The skull was set up at the foot of the flagstaff.
The national flag flew from the flagstaff.

usage.pattern: at the foot of the flagstaff

meaning: To wave arms or legs wildly without control
trick: FLAIL - you flail when you fail to swim.
examples: I had to flail over the white wash in the cold ocean.
Don't flail your arms if you fall into water.

meaning: Came off in small thin pieces
trick: FLAKED - like old paint flakes off a wall.
examples: Hate flaked from my soul like used-up snake skin.
The old paint flaked off the door.

meaning: Small, thin, light pieces of something
trick: FLAKES - corn flakes, snow flakes.
examples: Flakes of plaster rained down on her from the ceiling.
Snow flakes fell softly on the road.

meaning: Breaking or peeling off in small dry pieces; also (informal) unreliable
hindi: पपड़ीदार, झड़ने वाला; भरोसे लायक़ नहीं (बोलचाल)
trick: FLAKY = full of flakes - dry skin.
examples: He ran his thumb over her flaky eyebrows.
Use cream for your flaky skin in winter.

meaning: Very confident, bold and showy, attracting attention
trick: FLAMBOYANT - like a FLAMing BOY dressed to stand out.
examples: Dostum was the flamboyant Uzbek commander.
The singer wore a flamboyant gold jacket.

meaning: Tall pink wading birds with long legs and necks
trick: FLAMINGOS - pink like FLAMEs.
examples: His cousin was flogged once for painting flamingos.
We saw hundreds of flamingos at the lake.

meaning: Had something on one or both sides
hindi: दोनों ओर से घिरा, किनारे पर
trick: FLANK = the side; FLANKED = with things at the sides.
examples: The track was flanked by knee-high grass.
The president was flanked by two guards.

meaning: Is on one or both sides of something; also (noun) the sides of something
hindi: किनारे पर है, दोनों ओर है
trick: FLANK = side - grass flanks the road.
examples: Tall grass flanks the road on both sides.
A row of shops flanks the main street.

meaning: Trousers made of a soft woollen cloth; also small cloths for washing the face
hindi: ऊनी पतलून; मुँह पोंछने का कपड़ा
trick: FLANNELS - soft FLANNEL fabric trousers.
examples: A young man in gray flannels was gazing hard at me.
He wore white flannels to the cricket match.

meaning: Moved up and down or side to side quickly, often noisily
trick: FLAPPED - a bird flapped its wings.
examples: Sandals with ragged straps flapped back and forth.
The flag flapped in the wind.

meaning: A sudden short burst of a feeling or light
trick: FLARE - like a sudden flame flaring up.
examples: A flare of pride caught her off guard.
She felt a flare of anger at his words.

meaning: Showing no emotion or interest; also level and smooth
trick: FLAT voice/look = no ups and downs, like a flat line.
examples: Her eyes settled on Mariam in a flat, unblinking way.
He answered in a flat voice.

meaning: Pressed or pushed down so it lay flat
trick: FLATTENED - made flat, like a rolled roti.
examples: The rain flattened Aziza's long hair.
The storm flattened the crops.

meaning: Ran away from a place or danger
trick: FLED = past of FLEE; the thief fled.
examples: His getaway driver had fled the scene.
The family fled the war.

meaning: A soft, warm, fuzzy fabric used for jackets and hats; also a sheep's wool coat
hindi: ऊनी गरम कपड़ा; भेड़ का ऊन
trick: FLEECE - soft like a sheep's fleece.
examples: I wore a hoodie and a fleece hat.
She zipped up her fleece jacket.

meaning: Running away from a place or situation
trick: FLEEING - like a FLEA jumping away.
examples: Pam dealt with it by fleeing the scene.
People were fleeing the burning building.

meaning: Lasting for a very short time
trick: FLEETING - like a fleet of ships passing by quickly.
examples: He shot Mariam a fleeting look.
I caught a fleeting glimpse of the star.

meaning: A quick, light movement, especially of the hand or wrist
trick: FLICK - flick a switch, quick and light.
examples: With a flick of her wrist, she can draw hot or cold water.
Lights come on with a flick of a switch.

meaning: A short, sudden feeling or sign of something; also an unsteady light
trick: FLICKER - like a candle flickering for a moment.
examples: Mariam felt a flicker of jealousy.
A flicker of hope crossed his face.

meaning: Removing something with a quick, light movement of the finger
trick: FLICKING - flick crumbs off the table.
examples: The driver said this while flicking cigarette ash out the window.
She was flicking crumbs off her shirt.

meaning: Thin and easily torn or broken; also weak and unconvincing
trick: FLIMSY - flimsy paper flaps in the wind.
examples: The wives each had on a flimsy black scarf.
The flimsy tent blew away in the storm.

meaning: To throw something hard or carelessly
trick: FLING - fling the ball far away.
examples: Khadim was known to fling bits of calf intestine at passersby.
Don't fling your clothes on the floor.

meaning: Short, casual romantic relationships (informal)
trick: FLINGS - a love you fling away after a while.
examples: Being with one woman has been more rewarding than all my flings.
He had a few flings in college before he got married.

meaning: Moving something quickly to and fro; also behaving as if attracted to someone, playfully
trick: Old sense: FLIRT = flick. Mollie was flirting (flicking) her tail.
examples: Mollie strolled into the yard, flirting her long tail.
The horse kept flirting its tail to keep the flies away.

usage.pattern: flirting something (old use) / flirting with someone

meaning: To go or gather somewhere in large numbers; also a group of sheep or birds
trick: FLOCK - sheep flock together.
examples: As the saying goes, birds of a feather flock together.
Tourists flock to Goa every winter.

meaning: Beaten hard with a whip or stick as punishment
trick: FLOGGED - FLOG sounds like 'flap' of a whip.
examples: His cousin had been publicly flogged once for painting flamingos.
In the past, thieves were flogged in public.

meaning: A punishment of being beaten with a whip or stick
trick: FLOGGING - the whip's flog-flog sound.
examples: Any animal caught singing it was given a flogging.
Public flogging is banned in many countries.

meaning: Gates that hold back water; opening them = suddenly letting many similar things happen
trick: Open the FLOODGATES - a flood follows.
examples: His record broke open the floodgates by proving it possible.
The new law may open the floodgates to more cases.

meaning: Soft and hanging down loosely
trick: FLOPPY - floppy ears flop down.
examples: He kept tossing the floppy locks of his hair.
The puppy has big floppy ears.

meaning: Cleaning between the teeth with a thin thread
trick: FLOSSING - floss = thread for teeth.
examples: Meanwhile, you're stuck at home flossing your cat.
The dentist said flossing every day is important.

meaning: Struggling badly and not knowing what to do
trick: FLOUNDER - a fish flopping about on land.
examples: Their economy was floundering.
I was floundering from one high to the next.

meaning: Fine powder made by grinding wheat or other grain, used for bread
trick: FLOUR ≠ flower: you bake with flour.
examples: She searched for flour and made fresh dough.
Mix the flour with water to make roti dough.

meaning: Grew or developed well and strongly
trick: FLOURISHED - FLOURish like a FLOwer in bloom.
examples: Terrible wickedness now flourished on Animal Farm, they said.
Her business flourished after the move to the city.

meaning: Openly breaks or ignores a rule or law
hindi: खुलेआम तोड़ता है, अवहेलना करता है
trick: FLOUTS ≠ flaunts - he FLOUTS the rules, he FLAUNTS his car.
examples: He flouts the basic principles of the community without regret.
My neighbour flouts the parking rules every day.

meaning: Soft, light bits or tufts of something, like snow, fur or cotton
trick: FLUFFS = little puffs of fluff, like cotton balls.
examples: Silvery fluffs of snow were melting off the branches of tall elms.
Fluffs of cotton were stuck to her sweater.

meaning: Soft, light and full like fur or cotton; also (informal) light and silly, not serious
trick: FLUFFY = like a fluffy puppy - soft, and not serious.
examples: I wasn't fluffy.
The kitten has soft, fluffy fur.

meaning: Something good or surprising that happens by pure luck, not skill
trick: FLUKE = 'flew' in by luck.
examples: If by some fluke the knife didn't do its job, they started again.
His first goal was just a fluke.

meaning: Failed an exam, course or training (informal); with "out" = was made to leave for failing
trick: FLUNKED = 'flop + sunk' - your marks sank.
examples: Brown hit his targets but missed the time, and he flunked out of training.
He flunked his maths test last week.

usage.pattern: flunk something / flunk out of something

meaning: Failing an exam, course or training (informal)
trick: FLUNKING = flopping and sinking in school.
examples: She told me I was flunking out.
He is flunking chemistry this term.

usage.pattern: be flunking something / be flunking out of something

meaning: (Of a light) giving bright white light from a glowing tube; also very bright and glowing in colour
trick: FLUORESCENT = 'floor' of the office lit by 'cent'-ury-old tube lights.
examples: I was staring at the fluorescent lights in the hospital ceiling.
She wore a fluorescent yellow jacket on her bike.

meaning: Quick, sudden and nervous or restless
trick: FLURRIED = like a flurry of snow - quick and jumpy.
examples: Small waves were lapping the hot sand in little, flurried gasps.
She gave a flurried wave and ran to the bus.

meaning: (Of the face or skin) turned red from heat, anger, effort or embarrassment
trick: FLUSHED = blood FLUSHES into your cheeks.
examples: When Nana saw the bowl, her face flushed red.
His cheeks were flushed after the long run.

meaning: Nervous and confused, especially because of hurry or pressure
trick: FLUSTERED = flushed + cluttered mind.
examples: Having found nothing, he seems flustered.
She got flustered when the teacher asked her a question.

meaning: Covered with fly eggs, so dirty and rotten; also very shabby
trick: FLYBLOWN = flies have blown (laid eggs) all over it.
examples: Mariam saw small mounds of flyblown garbage littering the street.
The flyblown meat at the stall smelled terrible.

meaning: Printed sheets of paper handed out or left around to give a message or advertise something
trick: FLYERS fly from hand to hand in the street.
examples: The message was also written in flyers, tossed into the streets.
They handed out flyers for the new shop.

meaning: A young horse or donkey
trick: FOAL sounds like 'foal-low' - it follows its mother.
examples: Clover never quite got her figure back after her fourth foal.
The foal stood up on wobbly legs.

usage.pattern: a foal / give birth to a foal

meaning: Young horses or donkeys
trick: FOALS follow their mothers in the field.
examples: Clover, where are those four foals you bore?
Two foals were playing in the field.

meaning: Material that gives people something to use or talk about; also dry food for farm animals
trick: FODDER = FOOD-er for cows - and for gossips.
examples: Laila didn't want to give these women any more gossip fodder.
The farmer stored fodder for the cows.

meaning: Very thin, shiny metal sheet used to wrap food; also (verb) to stop someone's plan
trick: FOIL = shiny wrap - foil the chocolate, keep it safe.
examples: He would bring Mariam chocolate candy wrapped in foil.
Mum wrapped the sandwiches in foil.

meaning: To force someone to accept something they do not want
trick: FOIST sounds like 'FORCED' - forced on you.
examples: People tried to foist their ideas on me.
Don't foist your old clothes on your little brother.

meaning: Touching or stroking gently and lovingly
trick: FONDLING = being FOND and handling gently.
examples: The child sat fondling the puppy's soft ears.
She was fondling the old ring her mother gave her.

meaning: Bold in a foolish way; taking silly risks
trick: FOOL + HARDY = a fool who thinks he's tough.
examples: He had a foolhardy faith that she was carrying a boy.
It was foolhardy to swim in that storm.

meaning: Low hills at the bottom of a mountain range
trick: FOOT-HILLS = hills at the foot of the mountains.
examples: Long ago, in the Himalayan foothills, there lived a king.
We camped in the foothills before the climb.

meaning: Ordered someone not to do something (past of forbid)
trick: FORBADE = FOR-BAD: said 'it's bad, don't'.
examples: On the doctor's advice, I forbade him to sit up beside the body.
Her father forbade her to go out at night.

usage.pattern: forbid someone to do something / forbid something

meaning: The front part; in a clear, noticeable position ("to the ...")
trick: FORE = before = in front (golfers shout 'Fore!').
examples: His white mustache was well to the fore.
New leaders have come to the fore this year.

usage.pattern: to the fore / come to the fore

meaning: Giving a feeling that something bad will happen; also (noun) such a feeling
trick: FORE + BODING = a bad sign BEFORE it happens.
examples: They were so tall, so foreboding, Jalil's walls.
The dark clouds looked foreboding.

meaning: The finger next to the thumb; index finger
trick: FORE-FINGER = the finger at the front.
examples: He squeezed his eyes with his thumb and forefinger.
She pointed with her forefinger.

meaning: Certain from the start; decided before it happens
trick: FORE-GONE = gone (decided) before it begins.
examples: They ignore their own perceptions to fit foregone conclusions.
The win was a foregone conclusion.

meaning: A lock of hair growing just above the forehead, especially on a horse
trick: FORE-LOCK = the lock of hair at the front.
examples: He set his ears back and shook his forelock several times.
The pony's forelock fell over its eyes.

meaning: Most important or first; above all
trick: FORE + MOST = most in front.
examples: Foremost among my many weaknesses is that I can't refuse you.
First and foremost, be kind.

usage.pattern: foremost among something / first and foremost

meaning: To know or guess that something will happen before it does
trick: FORE + SEE = see before.
examples: It was possible to foresee that the coming winter would be hard.
Nobody could foresee the problem.

meaning: That can be known or expected ahead; for as long as one can tell (with "future")
trick: FORESEE + ABLE = what you are able to see ahead.
examples: I was to have no friends for the foreseeable future.
Prices will stay high for the foreseeable future.

usage.pattern: for the foreseeable future / foreseeable + noun

meaning: Said in advance that something would happen (past of foretell)
trick: FORE + TOLD = told before.
examples: The Republic which Major had foretold was still believed in.
The old woman foretold a hard winter.

meaning: To lose or give up something, often as a result of an action; also (noun) something lost this way
trick: FORFEIT = 'for-fit' - not fit any more, so you lose it.
examples: I wanted my competitors to hear my splits and forfeit their souls.
The team had to forfeit the match.

meaning: Giving up or losing something, often because of a choice
trick: FORFEITING = for-fitting: what doesn't fit, you lose.
examples: We know all the other options we're forfeiting.
He is forfeiting his holiday to finish the work.

meaning: To move ahead steadily with effort, make strong progress; also to make metal things or fake documents
trick: FORGE ahead = like hot iron pushed forward by a blacksmith.
examples: By running and then walking, I was able to forge ahead.
The company forged ahead with its plan.

usage.pattern: forge ahead (with something) / forge a link

meaning: Chooses to go without something he or she wants
hindi: त्याग देता है, छोड़ देता है
trick: FOR-GOES = he lets it GO.
examples: Jimmy Fallon forgoes his playoff tickets for the girl.
She forgoes dessert to stay healthy.

meaning: Sad and lonely, as if left alone; also hopeless
trick: FORLORN = for-lone: left alone and sad.
examples: Jalil looked at her with a forlorn expression.
The forlorn puppy waited by the gate.

meaning: A feeling of being sad, lonely and left alone
trick: FORLORN + NESS = the state of being forlorn.
examples: A forlornness would descend on her like a shroud.
The forlornness of the empty house made him cry.

usage.pattern: a forlornness / the forlornness of something

meaning: Remains of very old plants or animals that have turned to stone
trick: FOSSILS = fossilised - frozen in stone forever.
examples: My legs were stiff as fossils frozen in stone.
We saw dinosaur fossils at the museum.

meaning: A small hole dug by a soldier to shelter in during battle
trick: FOXHOLE = soldiers hide in a hole like a fox.
examples: When we're in a foxhole we usually aren't alone.
The soldier dug a foxhole before night fell.

usage.pattern: in a foxhole / dig a foxhole

meaning: Dogs trained to hunt foxes by smell
trick: FOX + HOUNDS = hounds that chase foxes.
examples: Jones will sell you and boil you down for the foxhounds.
The foxhounds ran across the field.

meaning: Weak and easily hurt or broken
trick: FRAGILE - written on boxes of glass: handle with care!
examples: Surprisingly, his fragile health held up that whole way.
Be careful, the vase is fragile.

meaning: Weak and thin, especially from age or illness
trick: FRAIL = so weak you might FAIL to stand.
examples: He moved over to the window: a smallish, frail figure.
My grandmother is old and frail now.

meaning: Units of money once used in France and still used in Switzerland
trick: FRANCS = money of FRANCe.
examples: He paid her twenty francs a day for food.
The ticket cost ten francs.

meaning: Wild with worry, fear or hurry
trick: FRANTIC = in a PANIC, running in FRANTIC circles.
examples: My mother was already frantic because she hadn't heard from him.
She was frantic when she lost her keys.

usage.pattern: be frantic (with something) / a frantic + noun

meaning: In a wild, hurried and worried way
trick: FRANTIC + ALLY = doing it in a panic.
examples: A hand appeared and frantically pulled at a cord.
He searched frantically for his phone.

meaning: Full of worry and tension; also full of (danger, problems)
trick: FRAUGHT = full of FRIGHT.
examples: Logic is little help in the fraught interplay of two people negotiating.
The meeting was fraught with tension.

usage.pattern: fraught with something / a fraught + noun

meaning: (Of cloth or rope) worn at the edges so threads come loose; also (of nerves) tired and tense
trick: FRAYED edges are AFRAID of falling apart.
examples: She saw the frayed ends of richly coloured tapestries.
His jeans were frayed at the bottom.

usage.pattern: frayed at the edges / frayed + noun

meaning: (Informal) being cold and unfriendly to someone so they stay away; ignoring them
trick: FREEZING someone OFF = giving them the cold shoulder.
examples: I've no reason for freezing him off.
She kept freezing me off after our fight.

meaning: Fast, busy and wild in an uncontrolled way
trick: FRENETIC = FRENzied + hecTIC.
examples: Families had flooded the city on their frenetic rounds to visit relatives.
Life in the city is frenetic.

meaning: Wild, excited and out of control
trick: FRENZIED = in a FRENZY.
examples: She watched scrap paper ride the winds in a frenzied, corkscrew motion.
The crowd gave a frenzied cheer.

meaning: A state of wild, uncontrolled activity or excitement
trick: FRENZY = like a FRENZied FRIENDs' party.
examples: The sand flies would go on a feeding frenzy.
There was a frenzy of shopping before the festival.

usage.pattern: a frenzy of something / in a frenzy

meaning: Paintings made on wet plaster on walls or ceilings
trick: FRESCO = Italian 'fresh' - painted on fresh plaster.
examples: The monks painted beautiful frescoes along the walls of their caves.
We saw old frescoes in the church.

meaning: A student in the first year of high school or college (US)
trick: FRESH-MAN = a fresh (new) student.
examples: My class schedule came the summer before freshman year.
He is a freshman at the state university.

meaning: To worry or be anxious about something
trick: FRET = you FRET and sweat.
examples: Oh, don't you fret about that.
Don't fret, we'll find your bag.

meaning: In a worried, restless way
trick: FRET + FULLY = full of fretting.
examples: He fluttered his hands fretfully.
The baby cried fretfully all night.

meaning: Worried a lot about something
trick: FRETTED = got fretful.
examples: She had fretted over what dress to wear.
He fretted about the exam all week.

meaning: Worrying about something again and again
trick: FRETTING = like a guitar FRET - you keep pressing on it.
examples: Mariam would sleep poorly, fretting that Jalil wouldn't come.
Stop fretting about the weather.

usage.pattern: be fretting about/over something / fretting that ...

meaning: A sudden feeling of fear
trick: FRIGHT = FRIGHTened.
examples: She still shivered with fright when he was like this.
The loud noise gave me a fright.

usage.pattern: with fright / give someone a fright

meaning: Very cold; also (of a person) cold and unfriendly
trick: FRIGID = cold like a FRIDGE.
examples: I became what I am today on a frigid winter day in 1975.
We jumped into the frigid lake.

meaning: Decorative edges of hanging threads on cloth; also the outer edges of an area or group
trick: FRINGES = the fringe (edge) of a shawl.
examples: It was a silk shawl with beaded fringes.
The curtains have golden fringes.

usage.pattern: with fringes / on the fringes of something

meaning: Not serious or important; silly
trick: FRIVOLOUS = FRIVOL = trivial.
examples: Commitment frees you from the unimportant and frivolous.
Don't waste money on frivolous things.

meaning: Playing and running about in a happy, lively way
trick: FROLIC = FROg + LICK - playful as a jumping frog.
examples: The days of innocent frolicking in the streets with Tariq had passed.
Children were frolicking in the waves.

meaning: A mass of small bubbles on a liquid or at the mouth
trick: FROTH = foam on the FRONT of the cup.
examples: There was froth at the corners of her mouth.
He blew the froth off his coffee.

usage.pattern: froth on something / froth at the mouth

meaning: Making or forming lots of small bubbles
trick: FROTHING = making froth.
examples: I can see the ocean below, frothing against the cliffs.
The milk was frothing in the pan.

usage.pattern: be frothing / frothing at the mouth

meaning: Pulled the eyebrows together to show worry, anger or dislike
trick: FROWNED = face turned down like a FROWN.
examples: Mariam frowned internally.
The teacher frowned at the noisy boys.

usage.pattern: frown at someone / frown upon something

meaning: Pulling the eyebrows together in worry, anger or dislike
trick: FROWNING = a down-turned face, opposite of smiling.
examples: She spotted Fariba, who was frowning.
Why are you frowning at me?

meaning: In a careful way that spends little money
trick: FRUGAL = eat FRUit only - spend little.
examples: The truest happiness lay in working hard and living frugally.
They live frugally to save for a house.

meaning: The point when a plan or hope becomes real
trick: FRUITION = the plan finally bears FRUIT.
examples: Despite my fantasizing, the reality never came to fruition.
Her dream finally came to fruition.

usage.pattern: come to / bring something to fruition

meaning: People who are running away or hiding, especially from the police
trick: FUGITIVE = Latin 'fugere' = to flee.
examples: At least three armed fugitives were holed up inside.
The police caught the fugitives at the border.

meaning: A dazed state where a person acts without fully knowing what they do; also a piece of music with repeated tunes
trick: FUGUE = FOG in the head.
examples: I soldiered on in a fugue state.
After no sleep, she worked in a fugue all day.

meaning: Felt about or handled something clumsily
trick: FUMBLED = fingers like FUMBLING thumbs.
examples: He fumbled in his pocket and produced a grimy bandage.
She fumbled with her keys at the door.

meaning: Feeling about or handling something clumsily
trick: FUMBLING = all thumbs.
examples: She felt the driver's fingers fumbling for a grip at her shoulder.
He was fumbling for the light switch.

meaning: Was very angry, often quietly
trick: FUMED = smoke (fumes) coming out of your ears.
examples: They passed their snorkels back and forth with ease, while I fumed.
She fumed about the late train.

meaning: Strong, often harmful smoke or gas
trick: FUMES = smoky FUMEs from a pipe.
examples: The mask protected me from toxic fumes.
Car fumes make the air dirty.

meaning: Cleaning a place with chemical smoke or gas to kill insects or germs
trick: FUMIGATION = filling with FUMES to kill bugs.
examples: I placed a fumigation mask over my face.
The house was closed for fumigation.

meaning: Caused by or like a fungus
trick: FUNGAL = from FUNGus (mushrooms, mould).
examples: My sweat blossoms like a fungal growth.
He has a fungal infection on his foot.

meaning: Sending something (like money or weapons) to a place through a narrow route (US spelling)
trick: FUNNEL = pour it all through one narrow tube.
examples: The West could prove they weren't just funneling arms into Afghanistan.
They were funneling money into the project.

meaning: A place that is extremely hot; also a large enclosed fire used to heat buildings or melt metal
trick: FURNACE = FIRE in a box.
examples: It was like a furnace outside, with the sunlight on the sand.
The room was a furnace in May.

usage.pattern: like a furnace / a blast furnace

meaning: (Of the brow or face) wrinkled with deep lines from worry or thought
trick: FURROWED = lines like FURROWS in a ploughed field.
examples: His face furrowed in concentration.
She furrowed her brow at the hard question.

meaning: Deep lines on the face, especially the forehead; also long cuts made in the ground by a plough
trick: FURROWS = ploughed lines on a field - or a forehead.
examples: The furrows from his brow clear.
Worry left deep furrows on her forehead.

meaning: Very strong anger
trick: FURY = FURIOUS.
examples: The fury that churned within me that day was indescribable.
She shouted in fury at the driver.

meaning: To join two or more things into one; also to melt together
trick: FUSE = FUSION - two become one.
examples: Orwell tried to fuse political purpose and artistic purpose into one whole.
The song fuses jazz and folk.

usage.pattern: fuse something with/and something / fuse into one

meaning: Having no chance of success; pointless
trick: FUTILE = Future? NIL.
examples: We huddled tight to get warm, but it was futile.
It is futile to argue with him.

usage.pattern: be futile / it is futile to do something

meaning: The fact of having no use or purpose
trick: FUTILITY = being FUTILE.
examples: The futility of what was happening took me by the throat.
He saw the futility of fighting.

usage.pattern: the futility of something / of doing something

meaning: A thin mattress used on the floor or as a fold-out bed
trick: FUTON = FOOT-ON the floor bed.
examples: You're sleeping on a smelly futon and counting coins.
The guest slept on a futon in the living room.
